newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan Q&A -- Nominal fed funds rate Part VII.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan Q&A -- Nominal fed funds rate Part VII.

text.p: Following are excerpts from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's question-and-answer session the Senate Banking Committee with after the second day of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.

Sen. Sarbanes (D-Maryland): " ... Turning to the real interest rate question ... I'm struck by all these articles that are being written about you and they all seem to take the view that unless you raise interest rates, the open market committee is somehow falling down on the job ... the fact of the matter is with the inflation dropping just by keeping the fed funds rate where it is nominally in effect you are raising the real federal funds rate. Is that not the case?"

Sarbanes: "I think it's very important that there be an understanding that with inflation dropping, leaving the fed funds rate where it is raises the real fed funds rate and therefore is a restraining action with respect to the economy."

Greenspan: "That's the reason why I mentioned in my prepared remarks that movements in the nominal fed funds rate are routine aspects of monetary policy. We are making monetary policy every day by what we do and what we do not do. And we are aware of the process by which the elements of various structures of rates are affected by what we do or what we do not do. Obviously our awareness of the federal funds rate in real terms rising is something of our general policy understanding. So the notion that the only time that monetary policy changes is when we change the funds rate or the discount rate is not correct. It's a continuous process and one of the reasons why it's important to recognize that what we do, in a routine sense, is that we are doing it all the time and that's why it's the fundamental outcome of the policy that matters, not every individual particular move."

Sarbanes: "I would like to draw you out a bit just to get some of your thinking what you expect the impact on the international monetary system to be of the European monetary union? How significant is that in its potential impact?"

Greenspan: "It's fairly obvious that a single currency in the European community will enhance their ability to function in the same manner that the single currency in the 50 states of the U.S. allows us to function. It's going to create differences in the elements of the adjustment process within Europe, and to the extent that it enhances Europe's ability to become an effective world competitor, it's going to help us, not hinder us because what all the post WWII evidence, not to mention pre-war evidence, suggests, is that the greater the real growth in trade, the greater the ability of globalization and integration...the better it is for everybody. We hope that struggles that they're making which are obviously considerable bring fruition and success."

Different senator: "I am concerned there might be more leverage in the market than we might be led to believe. I understand that home equity loans have risen fairly rapidly with the possible effect that the proceeds of the loans are going into fueling the market ... Is that right and what is your opinion on the concerns I have?"

Greenspan: "One interesting area where as you point out the loans are expanding rapidly and some of them are changing in nature from standard home equity loan where you dip into a little bit into your equity whereas now there are lots of loans that are becoming huge parts of equity and in certain instances more than what equity is left. There are some problems that are starting to emerge in there...it's still a very small part of the consumer markets and not something that we at this particular stage particularly concerned about."
Senator: "Do you have any concern that there is more leverage in the market than you might feel comfortable with?

Greenspan: If you are referring to the issue of stock market credit, so-called margin credit, there is no question that over the last couple of months margin credit has risen substantially...it's over $100 billion now...but when you take it as a percent to the market value of the stocks to which they apply, the ratio is still below where it was, for example, in early 1995. The ratio to the value of stocks, to be sure, has increased recently but it's still relative to the overall value. Still just a little over one percent."
